dataset.name: HackUMBC 2026 Career Pathways & Degree ROI
dataset.disclaimer: Synthetic data from a simulation for HackUMBC 2026. Nothing here describes real UMBC students, and every result is an association, not a causal promise.

steps: Every family is trained and scored on exactly the same rows.
Champion choice: each family is fitted on the years before 2021 (risk, time to degree) or 2022 (career, salary) and scored on that year. The simplest family within one percent of the best score wins.
Refit on all training years, calibrate (risk only, Platt scaling on 2022), then score once on the graduating classes of 2023 to 2026.
A model beats another only if the 95% bootstrap interval of its holdout improvement excludes zero.

champion.label: Linear model
champion.note: The champion beats the naive baseline on the test holdout (95% interval excludes zero). A simple linear model was good enough: no more complex family beat it by the validation tolerance. On the test holdout gradient boosting scored numerically better than the champion; the champion was fixed on the validation years, so it stays.

candidates.label: Naive baseline
candidates.kind: Training-set prevalence (the same probability for everyone)

candidates.label: Linear model
candidates.kind: Logistic regression on standardised features, Platt-calibrated

importance.metric: Drop in holdout AUROC when the column is shuffled

selection.metric: Mean validation AUROC over stages 0 to 6
selection.rule: Each family is fitted on the years before the validation year and scored on the validation year, a slice of the training years. The champion is the simplest family within the tolerance of the best validation score. The test holdout is never used.

card.name: Academic risk
card.predicts: The probability that a student ends up cooked: taking more than five years to graduate, or withdrawing from five or more courses in total. It is asked after 0 to 6 completed regular terms.
card.summary: Fitted on 1706 synthetic alumni who graduated 2015 to 2021, calibrated on the 2022 class (313 alumni) and tested once on 1181 alumni who graduated 2023 to 2026. Those counts are for the enrollment-only stage; later stages use the alumni still enrolled at that stage.
limitations: The data is synthetic, so the patterns describe the simulation, not real UMBC students.

The cooked label counts withdrawals, so once withdrawals are visible (after the first term) the model is partly reading the answer. The enrollment-only stage is the honest headline; later stages look better than the model really is.
Associations only: the model does not show that changing a habit changes the outcome.
Each stage only sees alumni who were still enrolled at that stage, so students who graduated early are never seen there.
About 15% of the test alumni were cooked, so a model that never warns anyone is right most of the time. Compare against the baseline.
should_not_be_used_for: Deciding whether a real student may enrol, stay enrolled or receive aid.
Labelling or ranking real people. It is a planning aid for exploring scenarios.
Any statement about real UMBC students. The data comes from a simulation.

card.name: Time to degree
card.predicts: A likely range for years from entry to degree: the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of similar alumni, after 0 to 6 completed regular terms. About half of alumni should land inside the range.
card.summary: Fitted on the same 1706 alumni as the risk model (2015 to 2021) and tested on the 2023 to 2026 classes.
limitations: The data is synthetic, so the ranges describe the simulation, not real UMBC students.
Ranges are conditional quantiles from alumni who graduated; students who left without a degree are not in the data.
Associations only, not causal effects of taking more or fewer credits.
The range is meant to hold about half of outcomes, not to guarantee any one student's date.

card.name: Career destination
card.predicts: Where alumni with a similar degree record went first: Employed, Continuing education or Still seeking. The output is three probabilities, not a verdict.
card.summary: Fitted on 1692 synthetic alumni who graduated 2015 to 2022 and tested on 997 who graduated 2023 to 2026.
limitations: The data is synthetic, so the patterns describe the simulation, not real UMBC students.
No Response (480 alumni) means unknown, not unemployed. It is excluded and never treated as an outcome. Military (31 alumni) is too small to be a class and is also excluded.
Employed is 80% of labelled alumni, so the models rarely pick the smaller classes as their top guess. Read the probabilities, not the label.
Alumni who answered the survey may differ from those who did not.
The internship, credential and engagement counts are what alumni recorded by graduation. Moving them in the lab shows how outcomes differ across similar alumni, not what an intervention would do.

card.name: First-job salary
card.predicts: A likely range for first-job annual salary in nominal dollars: the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of similar employed alumni.
card.summary: Fitted on 1369 employed synthetic alumni who graduated 2015 to 2022 and tested on 778 who graduated 2023 to 2026.
limitations: The data is synthetic, so the ranges describe the simulation, not real UMBC salaries.
Only employed alumni have a first salary (2147 alumni), so the answer is what a first salary looked like if employed.

Salaries are nominal dollars of each graduating year and rose over time (median $71,000 for the 2015 class, $83,750 for 2022). Graduation year is not a feature, so the model blends years and no cross-year dollar comparison is meant.
On the holdout the champion's median is too low by $8,889 on average; those classes graduated after every training class.
R-squared is below zero on the holdout: predicting one average salary for everyone explains the holdout better than the model does in squared-error terms.
